purpose: De-identified linked HTOPS cohort ledger connecting April expense difficulty to June household burdens and institutional confidence while preserving the retrospective timing, selection, attribution, remedy, and later-action limits.

events.geography: United States; April and June 2025 HTOPS public-use linked respondent cohort
events.date_precision: April survey wave; expense difficulty refers to the reported survey period and June outcomes are a later wave, not a dated bill or institutional decision
events.denominator: 6,564 exact SCRAMID-linked respondents; April expense-difficulty valid n=2,582 and not-difficult valid n=3,957 for food insufficiency; June outcome-specific valid counts vary
events.method: Exact SCRAMID intersection of April and June 2025 HTOPS public-use files; April PWEIGHT applied to linked respondents for descriptive cross-lagged shares; no attrition-adjusted longitudinal weighting or causal estimation
events.missingness: The public-use bridge does not disclose a dated bill, responsible actor, usable alternative, effort, remedy, payment, account correction, prior trust, attribution, political action, switching, or exit; expense difficulty is self-reported and outcome reference periods differ
events.exposure: Respondents reported difficulty with household expenses in April; among the linked cohort, the difficult group had higher June shares unable to pay an energy bill, reporting food insufficiency, and reporting recent household job loss
events.alternatives_before_action: Job, food, benefit, credit, housing, medical, family, and non-use alternatives are not observed in this specific cross-lag record
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: April expense difficulty is followed descriptively by June food insufficiency at 12.3% versus 1.1%, inability to pay an energy bill at 21.4% versus 2.2%, and recent household job loss at 11.7% versus 2.9% among difficult versus not-difficult linked respondents
events.choice_or_response: The linked panel measures later household conditions and confidence in Congress, but does not identify the respondent's concrete adaptation, complaint, benefit route, or political action
events.person_or_actor_with_control: The responsible actor and decision-maker are not identified; household and institutional control remain unspecified
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: No event-specific institutional response, remedy, payment, correction, or benefit adequacy is measured; June confidence in Congress is a judgment endpoint, not a remedy
events.immediate_outcome: The same linked respondents are observed in a later wave on household material burdens and confidence in multiple institutions. High confidence among difficult versus not-difficult respondents was 17.2% versus 16.9% for Congress, 24.3% versus 30.8% for the presidency, 57.9% versus 71.9% for the military, 44.6% versus 62.9% for police, 29.2% versus 38.3% for the Supreme Court, 42.8% versus 52.0% for public schools, and 57.7% versus 69.6% for statistical agencies
events.protected_outcome: No protected household or political outcome is verified; the cross-lag shows differentiated burden and near-similar institutional confidence, not recovery
events.sacrificed_outcome: Food, energy, and work security may remain exposed, but the record cannot assign the later burdens to the April difficulty or identify what was sacrificed
events.cost_risk_transfer: The panel makes later household burden visible but does not identify whether costs shifted to a provider, employer, agency, creditor, family member, or the household
events.later_outcome: Later household burden and confidence are observed descriptively; durable security, trust change, political action, switching, and exit remain open
events.meaning_and_attribution: Institution-specific confidence is observed as a later judgment profile: Congress is nearly flat while several other institutions show lower confidence in the difficult group. There is no prior confidence, actor attribution, fairness interpretation, or event-linked meaning change
events.public_or_collective_response: No complaint, contact, organizing, vote, protest, or collective response is linked to the expense episode in this ledger
events.counterexample: Material pressure can be associated with much higher later household burden and selective institutional-confidence gradients without one universal political judgment; Congress is nearly flat while other targets differ
events.source_and_uncertainty: Retained HTOPS cross-lagged panel audit, analysis/projects/us-cost-trust-politics/data/htops-2025-cross-lagged-panel-audit.json; April PUF and June PUF hashes are preserved in the audit. Shares are associative, selected linked-wave comparisons with non-aligned reference periods, not causal effects or individual recovery records

arrows.to: June food insufficiency, energy-bill inability, and household job loss
arrows.evidence: The same SCRAMID-linked respondents are compared across April and June; weighted shares are 12.3% versus 1.1% for food insufficiency, 21.4% versus 2.2% for inability to pay an energy bill, and 11.7% versus 2.9% for recent household job loss
arrows.counterexample: The later burden may reflect selection, intervening shocks, reference-period mismatch, or other household conditions rather than the April expense report
arrows.remaining_gap: Dated bill or shock, responsible actor, household attribution, and causal timing

arrows.to: June confidence profile across Congress, presidency, military, police, Supreme Court, public schools, and statistical agencies
arrows.evidence: Among linked respondents, high confidence in the difficult versus not-difficult groups is 17.2% versus 16.9% for Congress, 24.3% versus 30.8% for the presidency, 57.9% versus 71.9% for the military, 44.6% versus 62.9% for police, 29.2% versus 38.3% for the Supreme Court, 42.8% versus 52.0% for public schools, and 57.7% versus 69.6% for statistical agencies
arrows.counterexample: These institution-specific differences do not establish causal trust change; the near-similar Congress share also shows that hardship does not produce one universal confidence response
arrows.remaining_gap: Prior confidence, attribution, fairness meaning, institution-specific issue judgment, and action

arrows.evidence: The retained cross-lag audit does not identify what respondents searched for, delayed, borrowed, stopped using, or accepted between waves
arrows.counterexample: A later burden does not reveal whether the household adapted successfully, lacked an alternative, or protected another currency
arrows.remaining_gap: Search, alternative availability, non-use, money/time trade-off, adaptation, and protected/sacrificed outcome

arrows.to: durable recovery, trust change, political action, switching, or exit
arrows.evidence: The two-wave screen has no event-level remedy, prior-to-later trust change, political action, switching, or exit outcome
arrows.counterexample: Similar confidence in Congress does not imply similar trust, blame, political action, or institutional exit
arrows.remaining_gap: Later persistence, recovery, trust, action, switching, and exit for the same episode

boundary: This ledger establishes a bounded same-respondent material-pressure-to-later-household-and-institutional-judgment bridge. It does not establish a dated causal shock, usable alternative, remedy, trust change, political action, recovery, switching, or exit.
storage_boundary: No raw HTOPS respondent or replicate file is retained in this ledger; only compact derived shares, denominators, hashes, and interpretation boundaries are represented.
